rows: Employers must manage workplace temperature as part of health and safety duties.
There is no single legal maximum working temperature for all workplaces.
Indoor workrooms should normally be at least 16°C, or 13°C for strenuous work.
Temperature should be reasonable for the work and the people doing it.
Clean and fresh air should be provided.
Local heating, cooling, ventilation or work changes may be needed.
Workers should be consulted about thermal conditions.
Controls should be reviewed during weather, process or occupancy changes.
A room thermometer reading alone does not prove that thermal conditions are suitable.
Conclusions require temperature, humidity, radiant heat, air movement, work rate, clothing, duration and worker evidence.
Heat stress can occur when the body cannot adequately control its internal temperature.
Work rate, air temperature, humidity, radiant heat and clothing affect heat stress.
Employers should assess workers exposed to high heat or heavy work.
Engineering controls can reduce heat at source or improve ventilation.
Work-rest schedules and cooler work periods can reduce exposure.
Workers need access to suitable drinking water and hydration arrangements.
Acclimatisation and individual susceptibility should be considered.
Symptoms and incidents should trigger immediate response and control review.
Air temperature or a drink-water station alone does not determine heat-stress risk.
Conclusions require environment, metabolic rate, clothing, duration, hydration, acclimatisation and health evidence.
Thermal comfort depends on environmental, work-related and personal factors.
Air temperature alone does not determine whether people are comfortable.
Humidity, air movement and radiant temperature affect comfort.
Work rate and clothing influence how workers experience temperature.
Employers should use worker feedback and workplace assessment.
Heat or cold sources can be separated or shielded where possible.
Local heating, cooling, ventilation and work organisation may improve comfort.
Changes should be checked to confirm they have improved conditions.
A thermostat setting does not prove thermal comfort for all workers or tasks.
Conclusions require environmental measurements, work rate, clothing, duration, location and worker-feedback evidence.
Musculoskeletal disorders can affect the back, joints, muscles and limbs.
Work can cause or worsen musculoskeletal symptoms.
Risk factors include force, repetition, awkward posture and prolonged activity.
Employers should identify hazardous tasks and assess the risks.
Work design and mechanical aids can reduce physical demands.
Job rotation or breaks may help when they genuinely reduce exposure.
Workers should be encouraged to report symptoms early.
Assessments and controls should be reviewed when work or symptoms change.
A reported pain score or job title does not establish work causation or exposure.
Conclusions require task, force, posture, frequency, duration, individual factors, controls and clinical evidence.
